steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Uterine Diseases focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.dosing: Standard clinical care protocol under medical supervision.
drug_classes.pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Uterine Diseases require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Uterine Diseases.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: GFR increases by 50% in normal pregnancy; adjust renal eliminated medications accordingly.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Screen for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy when pruritus occurs in 2nd/3rd trimesters.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Strictly utilize FDA Category A/B or well-characterized safe pregnancy registry medications.
special_populations.elderly: For postmenopausal hormone therapy, use lowest effective dose for shortest duration; transdermal preferred.

style_3_monograph.summary: What are uterine diseases? The uterus, or womb, is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy. Uterine diseases are conditions that affect the uterus. These diseases can be benign (not cancer) or malignant ( cancerous ). They may affect your menstrual periods, your ability to get pregnant , or the health of your reproductive organs. Some types of uterine diseases include: Adenomyosis. Tissue that usually lines the uterus grows on the outside walls. Cervicitis. Swelling or inflamed tissue of the cervix. The cervix is the lower part of the uterus. Endometrial hyperplasia. An overgrowth of normal cells inside the uterus. Endometriosis . Tissue like the lining of the uterus grows in other places in your body. Uterine prolapse. The uterus drops in to the vagina due to weakened pelvic muscles. This can happen after a few vaginal births, menopause, or because of obesity. What causes uterine diseases? Various factors can cause uterine diseases. These can include hormonal imbalances, thyroid problems , fibroids , polyps, cancer, infection, or pregnancy. What are the symptoms of uterine diseases? Your symptoms will depend on the type of uterine condition you have. The first sign of a problem with the uterus may be abnormal bleeding . Bleeding could occur between periods, be very heavy, or last much longer than usual. Other symptoms may include bleeding after sex or pelvic pain . How are uterine diseases diagnosed? To find out the cause of your symptoms, your health care provider may: Ask about your symptoms and medical history Do a pelvic exam Order blood tests or imaging tests Do a biopsy What are the treatments for uterine diseases? Treatment depends on the cause. It may include pain medicine, hormone therapy, or surgery. Your provider will work with you to choose the best treatment.
style_3_monograph.treatment: Most women have some adenomyosis as they get close to menopause. However, only a few will have symptoms. Most women do not need treatment. Birth control pills and an IUD that has progesterone can help decrease heavy bleeding. Medicines such as ibuprofen or naproxen can also help manage pain. Surgery to remove the uterus (hysterectomy) may be done in women with severe symptoms.
